links.note: 41 calls the householder the துணை who stands on the good path (நல்லாற்றின் நின்ற) for 'the three' (இயல்புடைய மூவர்), whom Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar take as the other three orders of life (Kalaignar instead reads parents, spouse and children). 1036 says that if the ploughmen's hands fold (கைம்மடங்கின்), even those who say 'we have let go of desire' (விட்டேம் என்பார்) have no standing (நிலை). On the older commentators' reading both verses make the renouncer's state depend on someone who stays in the world and produces: the householder in Book 1, the farmer in Book 2.

41 makes the householder the support of the three, read by Parimelazhagar as the other orders, ascetics included. 263 asks, with கொல், whether 'the others' (மற்றையவர்கள்) have forgotten தவம் because they want to provide for the renounced (துறந்தார்க்குத் துப்புரவு வேண்டி); Parimelazhagar glosses 'the others' as householders. The Thavam chapter thus looks at the same arrangement from the ascetic side: the householder's support of renouncers is given as the reason he does no austerity himself.

41 names the householder the support of 'the three of proper nature' (இயல்புடைய மூவர்); 42 repeats the frame இல்வாழ்வான் என்பான் துணை and adds three more: துறந்தார், துவ்வாதவர், இறந்தார். Parimelazhagar takes these as the abandoned, the poor and those who died with no one of their own, so the pair moves from the recognised orders to people with no claim on anyone. Pope and Kalaignar read துறந்தார் as ascetics, which would make 42 overlap 41 rather than extend it.

42 lists துவ்வாதவர், those who have nothing to eat or enjoy, among the people the householder supports. 226 says that ending the destroying hunger of those without means (அற்றார் அழிபசி தீர்த்தல்) is the place where a person who has gained wealth stores it (பொருள் வைப்புழி). 226 turns the duty stated in 42 into a claim about what wealth is for.

43 lists five quarters to be tended (ஐம்புலத்தாறு ஓம்பல்): ancestors, gods, guests (விருந்து), kin and oneself, and calls this the chief thing (தலை). 81 says that all of staying, guarding one's goods and living at home (இருந்தோம்பி இல்வாழ்வதெல்லாம்) is for the sake of tending guests and doing them good (விருந்தோம்பி வேளாண்மை செய்தற் பொருட்டு). One of the five items of 43 is taken up, with the same verb ஓம்பு, and made the purpose of the whole household.

43 puts kin (ஒக்கல்) among the five the householder must tend. 524, in the chapters on kingship, says that living so as to be surrounded by one's kin (சுற்றத்தால் சுற்றப்பட ஒழுகல்) is the fruit of having gained wealth. The household duty of Book 1 reappears in Book 2 as the point of a ruler's prosperity.

44 says a life that fears blame and has பாத்தூண், food shared out, never sees its line fail (வழியெஞ்சல் எஞ்ஞான்றும் இல்). 227 uses the same compound: the one habituated to shared food (பாத்தூண் மரீஇயவனை) is hardly touched by the disease called hunger. Both attach a protective result to the same practice, one for the descendants and one for the sharer himself.

44 promises an unfailing line (வழி) to the life that fears blame (பழியஞ்சி) and shares its food; Parimelazhagar reads the fear of blame as applying to how the wealth is earned. 112 says the prosperity of the person of rectitude (செப்பம் உடையவன் ஆக்கம்) does not decay and is a security to those who come after (எச்சத்திற்கு ஏமாப்பு). In both, wealth held without wrong is what lasts into the next generation.

44 names பாத்தூண், shared food, as the mark of the householder's life. In 1107 the lover says the embrace of the woman is like staying in one's own home and eating one's own after sharing it (தம்மில் இருந்து தமது பாத்து உண்டற்று). The Book of Love takes the householder's sharing meal as a standard of pleasure, where 44 gives it as a duty with a reward; the comparison is the speaker's, not a teaching.

45 says that if household life has love and virtue (அன்பும் அறனும்), that is its character and its fruit (பண்பும் பயனும்). 75 says the distinction reached by those who have had joy in this world is, 'they say', the result of a way of life settled in love (அன்புற்று அமர்ந்த வழக்கு); Parimelazhagar takes this as household life lived with love, rewarded with heaven. 75 spells out the பயன் that 45 only names.

46 asks what one who conducts household life in the way of virtue would gain by going to the outside way (புறத்தாற்றில் போஒய்ப் பெறுவது எவன்); Parimelazhagar and Pope take the outside way as renunciation. 348 says those who have renounced completely (தீரத் துறந்தார்) have reached the head, and the rest (மற்றையவர்) are confused and caught in the net. If புறத்தாறு is renunciation and the question in 46 is rhetorical, 46 denies the gain that 348 reserves for renouncers alone; if புறத்தாறு means only ways outside virtue, the conflict disappears.

47 says the one who lives household life according to its nature is first among all who strive (முயல்வாருள் எல்லாம் தலை). 266 says those who do தவம் are doing their own work and the rest (மற்றல்லார்), caught in desire, do what is futile (அவஞ்செய்வார்). On Parimelazhagar's reading of 47, where the strivers are those working to leave the senses, the householder is ranked above ascetics, while 266 counts everyone but the ascetic as wasting effort. Manakkudavar reads முயல்வார் as those who strive for wealth, and on that reading the two do not collide.

48 says a household life that keeps others on their path (ஆற்றின் ஒழுக்கி) and does not slip from virtue has more endurance than those who do penance (நோற்பாரின் நோன்மை உடைத்து). 225 says the strength of the strong is enduring hunger, and that comes behind the strength of those who remove that hunger (மாற்றுவார் ஆற்றலின் பின்). Both rank the one who provides above the one who abstains, and both do it by granting the ascetic's own virtue, endurance, and awarding more of it to the provider.

48 gives household life more நோன்மை than those who do penance (நோற்பார்). 160 says those who fast as penance (உண்ணாது நோற்பார்) are great, but behind those who bear the harsh words others speak (இன்னாச்சொல் நோற்பாரின் பின்), using the same verb நோல் for both. The same comparison is made in the chapter on forbearance: an everyday virtue practised among people is placed above formal austerity.

49 says what is called virtue is household life, and 'that too' (அஃதும்) is good if it is not something others blame (பிறன் பழிப்பது இல்லாயின்). Parimelazhagar takes அஃதும் as renunciation and the blame as false conduct in ascetics (Manakkudavar keeps it on household life). 280 says neither shaving nor growing the hair is needed if one drops what the world has blamed (உலகம் பழித்தது ஒழித்து விடின்). On Parimelazhagar's reading the chapter on false ascetics works out the condition 49 states in passing: the renouncer's standing rests on being free of blame.

44 opens with பழியஞ்சி: the household life that fears blame and shares its food keeps its line. 49 calls household life virtue itself, then adds that it is good if there is nothing others blame (பிறன் பழிப்பது இல்லாயின்). On Manakkudavar's reading, where அஃதும் still refers to household life, 49 makes absence of blame the condition on the chapter's whole praise of the householder, which 44 had already built into its description.

50 says one who lives on earth as one should (வாழ்வாங்கு வாழ்பவன்) will be placed among the gods who dwell in the sky (தெய்வத்துள் வைக்கப்படும்). 388 says the king who does justice and protects will be set apart as இறை for the people (இறையென்று வைக்கப்படும்). The same passive, வைக்கப்படும், is used for both: a human being who fully does the duty of his station, householder or ruler, is ranked as divine by others. This edition prints 50's third word corruptly (வான்உநற்யும் for வானுறையும்).

50 places the person who lives rightly on earth (வையத்துள்) among the gods of the sky. 413 says those who have listening as food for the ear are, though on earth (நிலத்து), equal to the gods who are fed by oblations. Both verses set 'on earth' against the gods and say a human excellence closes the gap, right living in one case and learning by listening in the other.

51 defines the companion of life as the wife who has the qualities the home needs and is வளத்தக்காள், fitted to the means of the man who took her; Parimelazhagar glosses this as spending in line with his income. 478 says that even if the channel of income is narrow there is no ruin, so long as the channel of outgo is not wider (போகாறு அகலாக் கடை). The rule 478 gives a king for his treasury is the one 51 builds into the definition of a good wife.

52 says that if excellence of the home (மனைமாட்சி) is not in the wife, the life is nothing, whatever excellence it has (எனைமாட்சித் தாயினும் இல்). 750 says that whatever excellence a fort has (எனைமாட்சித் தாகியக் கண்ணும்), it is as nothing in those who lack excellence in action (வினைமாட்சி இல்லார்கண் இல்லது). The two share the phrase and the argument: the outward assets of a home or a fortress count for nothing without the quality of the person inside who runs it.

53 asks what is lacking if the wife has worth (இல்லதென் இல்லவள் மாண்பானால்) and what is there if she does not (உள்ளதென் ... மாணாக் கடை). 430 says those with understanding have everything, and those without it have nothing whatever they have (என்னுடையரேனும் இலர்). The same two-sided formula, one possession that makes all others count or not count, is applied to a wife's character in the home and to understanding in a ruler.

54 asks what is greater than a woman, if she has the firmness called கற்பு (கற்பென்னும் திண்மை உண்டாகப் பெறின்). 988 says poverty is no disgrace to a person, if he has the firmness called சால்பு (சால்பென்னும் திண்மை உண்டாகப் பெறின்). The second line is the same but for one word, so the book describes a woman's fidelity and a worthy person's character with the same term, திண்மை, a firmness that outweighs outward circumstances.

55 says that when the wife who worships no god but rises worshipping her husband says 'rain', it rains (பெய்யெனப் பெய்யும் மழை). 545 says rain and harvest together (பெயலும் விளையுளும் தொக்கு) belong to the land of the king who wields the sceptre as he should. In both, rain answers to a person keeping faith with a role, the wife in the house and the king over the land; 559 gives the reverse case, where the sky withholds rain from an unjust king.

55 praises a wife who does not worship a god (தெய்வம் தொழாஅள்) and worships her husband, and credits her with power over the rain. 2 asks what use learning is if the learned do not worship the feet of the one of pure knowledge (நற்றாள் தொழாஅர் எனின்), with the same verb in the same negative form. Read literally, 55 commends for the wife the not-worshipping that the first chapter treats as making a person's attainments useless. Parimelazhagar removes the conflict by reading 'other gods' (பிற தெய்வம்) and making the husband her god; the tension depends on taking தெய்வம் தொழாஅள் at face value.

56 defines the woman as one who guards herself (தற்காத்து), cares for her husband and guards the good name (சொற்காத்து) without flagging. 57 asks what guarding by confinement (சிறைகாக்கும் காப்பு) can do, and says the guard women keep by their own நிறை is the chief one. 57 explains why 56 makes her the subject of the verb 'guard': the guarding that counts cannot be done by anyone else.

56 includes guarding the well-founded word, the couple's good name (தகைசான்ற சொற்காத்து), in its definition of the wife. 59 says those whose home does not seek renown (புகழ்புரிந்த இல் இலோர்க்கு) cannot walk with a proud gait before those who deride them. Parimelazhagar connects them directly, saying 59 states the fault that follows when that good name is not kept: the husband's standing in public depends on it.

57 says guarding women by confinement achieves nothing and the guard kept by their own steadfastness (நிறைகாக்கும் காப்பு) is chief. 974 says greatness, like single-minded women (ஒருமை மகளிரே போல), exists only if one keeps hold of oneself (தன்னைத்தான் கொண்டொழுகின்). The self-guarding wife of 57 becomes, in Book 2, the model for how anyone keeps greatness: it cannot be conferred or enforced from outside.

57 treats நிறை as a guard that women themselves keep and sets it above any confinement. In 1251 the woman in love says the axe of desire breaks the door called நிறை, bolted with the bar of shame (நிறையென்னும் நாணுத்தாழ் வீழ்த்த கதவு). Both picture நிறை as a barrier held from the inside; the Book of Love speaker reports it giving way under desire, which is her experience in the moment and not a retraction of 57.

58 says women who 'obtain the one who obtained them' (பெற்றாற் பெறின்) gain great distinction in the world where the gods live (புத்தேளிர் வாழும் உலகு); Parimelazhagar supplies 'honour' and reads it as wives who revere their husbands. 50 says the man who lives on earth as he should is placed among the gods of the sky. The two adjacent chapters end on the same reward, one for the householder and one for the wife, each for fulfilling the household role.

59 says those whose home does not seek renown (புகழ்புரிந்த இல்) have no proud gait before those who deride them (இகழ்வார்முன்). 237 asks why those who cannot live with renown (புகழ்பட வாழாதார்) resent those who deride them (இகழ்வாரை நோவது எவன்) and not themselves. Both set புகழ் against இகழ்வார்: 59 says that without renown one has no answer to scorners, and 237 adds that the scorn is then one's own doing.

59 says that without a home that seeks renown there is no walking with a bull's (Parimelazhagar: lion's) proud gait, ஏறுபோல் பீடு நடை. 1014 says shame is an ornament to the worthy, and without it their பீடு நடை is a disease. The proud walk appears twice as something that must be earned by an inner or domestic quality, the household's good name in one verse and a sense of shame in the other.

60 says the excellence of the home is called its blessing (மங்கலம்) and the gaining of good children (நன்மக்கட் பேறு) its fine ornament. 61, opening the next chapter, says that of all things to be gained we know none like the gaining of children who know what should be known (அறிவறிந்த மக்கட்பேறு). 61 picks up the word மக்கட்பேறு from 60 and specifies what makes the children 'good': their understanding.
